justification_text:
The point estimates in the forecast at the three time horizons—one day, one week, and one month—are primarily influenced by the most recent trends and underlying drivers that affect the system or variable being predicted. For example, the one-day point estimate of 30.93 reflects a heavy reliance on short-term stability and continuity of the most recent observations, as changes are generally less pronounced over such a short time. By the one-week horizon, the point estimate of 30.85 assumes slightly higher chances of mean-reversion or small shifts in prevailing dynamics, which might represent normal short-term fluctuations. By the one-month horizon, the point estimate of 30.5 suggests a more noticeable leaning toward a longer-term correction or adjustment, reflecting the likelihood that larger patterns or trends could have more influence over such a time span.

The confidence intervals widen as the time horizon lengthens because uncertainty grows the further into the future we try to predict. Over one day, uncertainties are typically smaller, because sudden changes are less common on such a short timescale. For one week, greater uncertainty exists, as there is more time for unexpected factors to emerge and influence the outcome. Over the course of a month, even more variables could come into play, such as broader environmental changes, behavioral shifts, or the unfolding of trends not yet observable in the present data. This is reflected in the increasingly wider intervals as the forecast horizon extends.

Outside of the ranges presented, specific risks or events could drive outcomes beyond the stated intervals. For example, an unforeseen event—such as a major market shock, regulatory change, or significant environmental factor—could result in abrupt and outsized changes. These could invalidate the assumptions used to generate the estimates and lead to outcomes that are well outside the confidence intervals. Such events are difficult to predict with precision, which is why they represent tail risks rather than central scenarios in the provided forecast.
